lessons.title: Review — what the surface does not tell you
lessons.gloss: a second pass over four facts that the surface of a word or a page will not give you — an ending, an article, a letter, and a punctuation mark

segments.text: One word to start. What does pronto mean on its own? (Soon — and "ready", the sense English kept in prompt.)
Four things you met separately, gathered because they share a shape: in each one, the part you can see is not the part you should trust.
First. Pronto looks like a word about right now. It is about readiness, from promptus, "brought forth" — and "soon" is where readiness ended up.
Second. Lo siento and perdón both come out as English "sorry". The English does not divide them; the Latin does. One names your feeling, the other asks for their pardon.
Third. El agua looks masculine and is not. The article moved for sound; the object pronoun did not, and says la.

Fourth. The h on hermano looks like the h on hijo. It is not the same letter's history: one stood where a Latin f was breathed aloud for centuries, the other was put on the page long after the sound had gone.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: the mark that was designed, not inherited

segments.text: The ¿ belongs on that list too, from the other side.

It is not a survival. It was decided — the Spanish Royal Academy made it official in 1754, because Spanish leaves the words of a question where they were and something had to warn the reader in advance.

So the page is carrying a job that English hands to word order. Four inherited surfaces that mislead, and one deliberate surface that helps: worth holding together, because reading a language well is mostly knowing which surfaces to believe.

segments.prompt: Which of the two sorries asks the other person for something?

feedback.incorrect: Perdón — it asks for their pardon.

segments.prompt: El agua takes el. Which pronoun replaces it, and what does that prove?
acceptedResponses: la, and that agua is feminine

feedback.correct: The article bent for sound; the pronoun did not bend at all.
feedback.incorrect: La. The el is a sound rule, so the pronoun is the honest witness.

segments.prompt: Hijo and hermano both start with a silent h. Which one was once spoken aloud?
acceptedResponses: hijo, where the h stands for a latin f

feedback.correct: Hijo's h was a real breath; hermano's never was.
feedback.incorrect: Hijo. Its h replaced a Latin f that was genuinely pronounced; hermano's h is spelling only.

segments.prompt: Was the opening mark inherited from Latin, or decided by somebody?
acceptedResponses: decided, by the spanish royal academy in 1754
the royal academy decided it in 1754

feedback.incorrect: Decided — the Spanish Royal Academy made it official in 1754.

segments.text: Which is the honest witness to a noun's gender — the article or the object pronoun? (The pronoun.) Which of Spanish's two sorries is about fault and getting past people? (Perdón.) When was ¿ made official? (1754.) Was hermano's h ever a sound? (No.) And what does pronto mean on its own? (Soon, from "ready".)

lessons.title: Review — the five words of a leaving
lessons.gloss: the five words of a leaving, said again in order, and the five different places they came from

segments.text: Two to start. Say "the street." (La calle.) Say "the corner." (La esquina.)

Say the five in order and hear the distance grow at every step: la calle, la esquina, la huella, el puerto, el faro — the street, its corner, the mark left in the dirt, the water's edge, and the light still visible when the town is not.

Now the part worth a second visit. Not one of the five was built for this list. Calle was a cattle track, callis. Esquina is a shinbone, Germanic skina. Huella comes from a day spent treading wool, fullāre. Puerto is the Roman harbour, portus, twin to the puerta on land. And faro was an island, Pharos, with a fire on top of a tower.
Five ordinary nouns out of five unrelated quarries. That is the ratio you should expect from here on.

acceptedResponses: la calle, la esquina, la huella, el puerto, el faro

feedback.correct: Each one further out than the last.

feedback.correct: A corner is an edge, and so is a shin.

segments.prompt: El faro was a place before it was a thing. Which place?

segments.text: What was fullāre? (Treading cloth in a vat — the trampling that gave huella its footprint.) What does ob portum describe? (A wind standing toward harbour — an opportunity.) And what is a faro in a car park today? (A headlight.)

lessons.title: Review — the harbour, the light, and see you soon
lessons.gloss: the harbour, the light at its mouth, and the goodbye that says you will be back shortly

segments.text: The last two nouns of the run. Say "the harbour." (El puerto.) Say "the lighthouse." (El faro.)
A leaving needs a place and a time, and you have both.
The place: el puerto, the gate off the sea, and el faro, the light standing at its mouth. The time: hasta pronto — hasta, "until", and pronto, "soon".
Say the whole thing once, slowly, as one leaving:
El puerto. El faro. Hasta pronto.

Three words out of three different centuries and two different languages — a Roman harbour, a Greek island, and an Arabic preposition holding a Latin adjective. You can hear all of that now, which you could not at the start.

segments.instruction: el puerto, el faro, hasta pronto

segments.prompt: Name the harbour and the lighthouse in Spanish, in that order.

feedback.correct: The gate off the sea, and the light at its mouth.

segments.prompt: Say see you soon, and give the two words it is made of.
acceptedResponses: hasta pronto: hasta, until, and pronto, soon

feedback.incorrect: Hasta pronto — hasta is until, pronto is soon.

segments.text: Which of the two is the light, and which is the water? (El faro; el puerto.) And what does pronto promise? (Soon — you will be back shortly.)
